blocks.text: Sulfonamides are synthetic compounds derived from sulfanilamide; the book dates their discovery to Gerhard Domagk in 1932. They treat bacterial infections, mainly urinary tract and skin infections, by inhibiting the bacterial synthesis of folic acid, which is essential for DNA synthesis and growth. They act as competitive inhibitors and are bacteriostatic. They are usually taken by mouth; side effects include rashes, nausea, sensitivity to light and kidney damage.

blocks.alt: Two rows. Normal: PABA fits the active site of a bacterial enzyme and folic acid is made, leading to DNA and growth. With a sulfonamide: the look-alike drug takes the site, no folic acid is made and growth stops. A note explains competitive inhibition and why human cells are spared.
blocks.caption: Sulfonamides compete with PABA for a bacterial enzyme (original diagram for this topic).
blocks.long_description: Bacteria must build folic acid themselves, using para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA) as a building block, whereas humans absorb folate from food. Sulfonamides are structural look-alikes of PABA: they compete with it for the bacterial enzyme that makes folate, so less folic acid is made and the bacteria cannot make DNA or grow. This is competitive inhibition. The effect is bacteriostatic, leaving the immune system to clear the bacteria; combining sulfonamides with trimethoprim gives a stronger, bactericidal effect.

items: Bacteriostatic: they do not kill bacteria at once but stop their growth, so the immune system can destroy them.
Selective toxicity: bacteria must build folate themselves, while humans absorb it from food, so the drug starves bacteria of a vital nutrient and leaves human cells untouched.
Competitive inhibition: as look-alikes of para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA), they bind the bacterial enzyme that uses PABA to make folate, blocking the pathway.
Combined therapy: they are often combined with trimethoprim for a stronger, bactericidal effect.
Broad spectrum: they act against Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria and are used for urinary tract infections, acne and respiratory infections.

blocks.prompt: Why are sulfonamides selectively toxic to bacteria?
blocks.explanation: Bacteria must make folate from PABA, the step the drug blocks; human cells take folate from food and do not use this pathway.

items: Compete with PABA and block folate synthesis; often given with trimethoprim.
